newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Komercni funds to post 1996 accounting loss.
newsitem.headline: Czech Komercni funds to post 1996 accounting loss.

text.p: Czech Komercni Banka a.s. unit Investicni Kapitalova Spolecnost said on Monday that its two funds on the Prague Stock Exchange main market -- IPF KB and PF-IKS KB PLUS -- would post accounting losses in 1996.

Fund managers told a news conference that IPF will post a loss of around two billion crowns after a 15.6 million crown net profit in 1995, and PLUS will show a 500 million crown 1996 net loss after a 102 million crown net profit.
The losses will be incurred because of the way in which the Czech Republic's coupon privatisation process delivered shares to the funds at a nominal value of 1,000 crowns each.

Just as share trading began on the bourse in earnest in 1994, share prices generally dropped significantly from the arbitrary opening price assigned during the country's massive voucher-based programme.
Because no initial principle investment was made in the stock at its issue price, the situation resulted in accounting losses on assets even when funds were earning profits.
In order to smooth over this anomaly, many funds performed a one-off operation whereby they sold all shares in their portfolios and immediately bought them back.
Both of the Komercni funds, which are managed by Komercni unit Investicni a Kapitalova Spolecnost (IKS KB), said that this operation was the cause of their expected 1996 losses.
IPF fund manager, Vladimir Kuba, said that for his fund:
"The expected level of losses for 1996 is at most two billion crowns, which is fully covered by the capital fund of IPF at the level of 2.5 billion crowns."
PF PLUS manager Jindrich Vodenka also said that his fund would end the year in the red for the same reason.
"The results of the fund for the year 1996 will end, as a consequence of the over pricing of the shares, in a loss at an expected level of around 500 million crowns.
"This loss will be fully covered by the fund with an amount of 600 million crowns," added Vodenka.
